newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RTRS - NZ's new electoral system delivers indecision.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - NZ's new electoral system delivers indecision.

text.p: One thing emerged clearly on Sunday, a day after New Zealand's first election under a mixed member proportion (MMP) system -- there was no clear winner.

Critics say New Zealanders at the last election in 1993 threw out the decisive first-past-the-post (FPP) Westminster system, which invariably produces a winner on election night, for an indecisive system where the winners may not emerge for months, if at all.

Both Labour Party leader Helen Clark and Prime Minister Jim Bolger made justifiable claims of victory on Saturday -- Clark saying the majority voted for change by opting for the three main opposition parties while Bolger said his conservative National Party won most seats with 44.
Bolger said those, combined with New Zealand First's 17, meant more people voted for conservative policies than supported Labour with its 37 seats added to the left-wing Alliance's 13.

Clark, who has acted as though Labour won and she would become the country's first woman prime minister, pointed out one of the most glaring anomalies in the new system which has put New Zealand First leader Winston Peters in the pre-eminent position.
"This electoral system gives the bronze medal winner the power to appoint the gold medal winner and the silver medal winner," she told Radio New Zealand.
A leading constitutional lawyer, Mai Chen, told Reuters a crunch for forming a government will come when parliament reconvenes on December 13.
"That will be showdown at OK Corral," she said.
However, she believes a government will be forged by then.
"I think the politicians will understand that the electorate does not want another election in the near future and they will respond to that.
"Any politician who is seen to be precipitating such an election will find they are punished at the polls," she said
Governor-General Sir Michael Hardie Boys has said he is prepared to wait until next year for a new government to form.
However, he has indicated he would want a government formed soon after the long summer holiday in January.
Bolger is confident politicians will sort out a government.

"Sir Michael Hardie Boys won't I'm sure have to step in," he told Radio New Zealand. "The political leadership will determine what it is they agree on to form a majority in the house or a minority government."
Bolger noted minority governments were common in many countries including ones regarded as successful such as Sweden.

Chen said that while FPP was normally decisive it resulted in a hung parliament in 1993, and since then New Zealand had had the gamut of governments from bare majority to minority coalition -- without noticeable ill effects.

She said the New Zealand's new "Washminster" system -- a cross between the British Westminster and Washington government -- would reduce the power of cabinet and the executive and restore it more to parliament.

"People did want more democracy. They wanted politicians to listen more to what they had to say. I think the MMP system will deliver more democracy in that sense. The difficulty is whether democracy will become perhaps less coherent in legislation and perhaps less efficient in government."
She said MMP favoured more moderate policies and avoided the sharp swings of FPP, but once policies were in place they would be difficult to change.
A caretaker government had been in place for some years and "monumental change" to the economic framework was unlikely.
"There is no reason for panic whatsoever," she said.
